intro: Basil Nevinson is the cellist in Elgar’s piano trio, and the cello opens and closes his portrait. Between those two solos, a roomful of friends becomes an orchestra.

sections.label: Var 12 · Nevinson’s cello
sections.mNote: A solo cello sings over hushed lower strings

sections.label: Var 12 · The violins join
sections.mNote: Divided violins rise above the cello phrase

sections.label: Var 12 · The cello’s last word
sections.mNote: The orchestra falls quiet around the soloist

cues.title: Nevinson’s own instrument
cues.text: A solo cello begins molto espressivo, free to linger over its first two bars. Quiet violas and the other cellos support it. Then the whole cello section takes up the tune, still broad and singing.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 82, rehearsal 52: solo cello marked molto espressivo and ad libitum, followed by a tempo and largamente ed espressivo for the cello section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trio’s generous cellist
cues.text: Nevinson plays chamber music with Elgar on violin and Hew David Steuart-Powell at the piano. Elgar’s written tribute praises more than his playing: Nevinson puts his scientific and artistic skills at his friends’ disposal, wholeheartedly.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello, 1946), commentary on variation XII, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations. The Elgar Society confirms the trio: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: A private farewell
cues.text: The orchestra dwindles, and the cello has the last phrase. Elgar writes a long pause, then lets the soloist reach upwards once more over held lower strings. The final instruction is attacca: the Romanza follows without a break.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 86: diminuendo molto, solo cello, longa fermata, ritardando and attacca. The extra final bar is reserved for separate performances.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The cello keeps singing
transitions.how: The G-minor Andante contracts around the cello. Elgar writes diminuendo molto across the winds and strings; the flutes and oboes stop, then the bassoons and horns. The basses fall silent while the orchestral cellos hold a low note beneath the soloist’s last upward phrase and its long pause.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 86: successive wind releases, silent double basses, held orchestral cellos and the solo cello’s final phrase.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 82–86, rehearsal figures 52–54: solo cello, the orchestral answer and the return of the opening solo.

timeline.note: Solo cello sings above divided violas and a held note in the other cellos (p. 82).
All the cellos take up the tune with violas and basses; wind replies join them before the violins enter (pp. 82–83).
Divided violins join the melody over a quiet timpani roll and wind chords (p. 83).
Woodwind phrases weave around the long violin melody (p. 84).
The violins sing on their G strings above lower wind chords (p. 85).
Woodwinds join the rising strings; trumpets and trombones remain silent (pp. 85–86).
Elgar writes dim. molto as the winds fall silent and the cello returns to its solo (p. 86).
Solo cello recalls its opening phrase over divided violas and held cello notes (p. 86).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
